invariants: Splitting a factor never changes the product: every piece of the split multiplies the other factor, and the pieces add back to exactly the same total, which is what makes g4m check product decomposable at all.
misconceptions: Adding only some of the partial products, dropping or inventing a zero when factors carry tens, or letting a remainder reach or exceed the divisor.

widget.prompt: Place 2,822 beside the benchmark 50 × 6 = 300. Which conclusion uses the size comparison correctly?

options.label: 2,822 is wrong — it is about ten times too big
options.feedback: Correct — the estimate places the answer near 300, so an answer in the thousands means a place-value slip.

options.label: 2,822 is fine — estimates are never exact
options.feedback: Estimates are not exact, but they are close. Being ten times out is a different kind of error entirely.

options.label: The estimate is wrong because it is not 2,822
options.feedback: Rounding deliberately changes the numbers; it is expected to differ a little, not by a factor of ten.

options.label: Nothing can be concluded
options.feedback: A great deal can: an answer an order of magnitude from the estimate is almost always a misplaced digit.
